rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.stem:
(a) Draw the circuit diagram of an illuminated photodiode and its I-V charcteristics.
(b) How can a photodiode be used to measure the light intensity ?
rows.solution:
**(a) The circuit and the characteristic.**

*The circuit.* Draw a p-n junction with a **thin, transparent p-layer** so that light can reach the depletion region, and connect it to a battery in **reverse bias** — the p-side to the negative terminal, the n-side to the positive — in series with a microammeter. Light \(h\nu\) falls on the junction through the exposed p-face.

Reverse bias is not incidental; it is the whole design. It widens the depletion layer, sweeps the photo-generated carriers apart at once, and keeps the dark current down to the tiny reverse saturation current, so the *change* produced by light stands out clearly against it.

*The \(I\)-\(V\) characteristic.* Plot current against voltage with the **third quadrant** — reverse voltage, reverse current — as the working region. Draw several curves, one per illumination level \(I_1 < I_2 < I_3 < I_4\), each nearly **flat and parallel to the voltage axis** beyond a small reverse voltage, and each lying further from the axis as the illumination rises. The topmost (darkest) curve is the dark current.

The flatness matters: beyond a small bias the photocurrent is almost independent of the reverse voltage. Every carrier the light generates is already being collected, so raising the voltage cannot collect more.

**(b) Measuring light intensity.**

The photodiode works because a photon of energy \(h\nu \geq E_g\) absorbed in or near the depletion region creates an **electron-hole pair**. The junction field sweeps the two apart before they can recombine, and they appear in the external circuit as photocurrent.

The number of pairs created per second is proportional to the number of photons arriving per second, which is proportional to the intensity. Hence

\(I_{\text{photo}} \propto \text{intensity}\)

and the relation is **linear over a wide range**, which is what makes the device a measuring instrument rather than a mere detector.

So: reverse-bias the diode, read the reverse current on the microammeter, subtract the dark current, and the remainder is a direct measure of the illumination. Calibrating the meter once against known intensities turns it into a light meter — the arrangement used in camera exposure meters, optical-fibre receivers and light-operated switches.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem:
(a) Calculate the frequency of a photon of energy \(6.5 \times 10^{-19}\) J.
(b) Can this photon cause emission of an electron from the surface of Cs of work function 2.14 eV ? If yes, what will be maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectron ?
rows.solution:
**(a) The frequency of the photon.**

\(E = h\nu \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \nu = \dfrac{E}{h} = \dfrac{6{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-19}}{6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34}}\)

\(\nu = 9{\cdot}8 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}\)

For orientation, this corresponds to \(\lambda = c/\nu \approx 306\) nm — near ultraviolet, just beyond the violet end of the visible range.

**(b) Will it eject an electron from caesium?**

Convert the photon energy into electronvolts so that it can be compared with the work function directly:

\(E = \dfrac{6{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-19}}{1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}} = 4{\cdot}06\ \mathrm{eV}\)

Caesium has \(\phi_0 = 2{\cdot}14\) eV, and

\(E = 4{\cdot}06\ \mathrm{eV} > \phi_0 = 2{\cdot}14\ \mathrm{eV}\)

**Yes** — emission occurs.

**The maximum kinetic energy** follows from Einstein's photoelectric equation:

\(K_{\max} = E - \phi_0 = 4{\cdot}06 - 2{\cdot}14\)

\(K_{\max} = 1{\cdot}92\ \mathrm{eV} = 3{\cdot}08 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\)

**Two points worth making.** The word *maximum* is exact, not loose: only electrons right at the surface escape having given up nothing but \(\phi_0\). Electrons freed deeper in lose energy on the way out, so the emitted electrons fill a whole range from zero up to \(1{\cdot}92\) eV.

And caesium is chosen here for a reason — its work function of \(2{\cdot}14\) eV is among the lowest of all metals, which puts its threshold wavelength at \(hc/\phi_0 \approx 580\) nm, in the *yellow*. Caesium is one of the few metals that visible light can strip electrons from, which is why photocells are coated with it.

rows.subtopic: Refraction and Reflection of Plane Waves
rows.stem: Monochromatic light of wavelength 600 nm is incident from air on a water surface. The refractive index of water is 1.33. Find the (i) wavelength, (ii) frequency and (iii) speed, of reflected and refracted light.
rows.solution:
The single fact that organises this question: **frequency is set by the source and never changes on crossing a boundary.** The wave in the water is driven by the wave in the air at the interface, oscillation for oscillation, so the two must keep time. What changes is the speed, and with it the wavelength.

**The incident light.**

\(\nu = \dfrac{c}{\lambda} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}}{600 \times 10^{-9}} = 5 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}\)

**Reflected light** — it never leaves the air, so nothing about it changes:

| | Reflected |
|---|---|
| Wavelength | \(600\) nm, unchanged |
| Frequency | \(5 \times 10^{14}\) Hz |
| Speed | \(3 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) |

**Refracted light** — it travels in water, where \(\mu = 1{\cdot}33\):

Speed:

\(v = \dfrac{c}{\mu} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}}{1{\cdot}33} = 2{\cdot}26 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)

Frequency: **unchanged**, \(5 \times 10^{14}\) Hz.

Wavelength:

\(\lambda' = \dfrac{\lambda}{\mu} = \dfrac{600}{1{\cdot}33} = 451\ \mathrm{nm} \approx 450\ \mathrm{nm}\)

| | Refracted |
|---|---|
| Wavelength | \(451\) nm |
| Frequency | \(5 \times 10^{14}\) Hz |
| Speed | \(2{\cdot}26 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) |

**A consistency check worth doing**, because it is the one the question is really testing: \(v = \nu\lambda'\) must still hold in the water.

\(5 \times 10^{14} \times 451 \times 10^{-9} = 2{\cdot}26 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)

It does. Speed and wavelength fall by the same factor \(\mu\), leaving the frequency untouched — which is exactly why a diver sees no colour shift underwater. Colour is a matter of frequency, and the frequency of the light has not changed.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors
rows.stem: Draw the energy band diagrams for conductors, semiconductors and insulators. Which band determines the electrical conductivity of a solid ? How is the electrical conductivity of a semiconductor affected with rise in its temperature ? Explain.
rows.solution:
**The three band diagrams.**

Each is drawn as electron energy increasing upwards, with the filled **valence band** below, the empty **conduction band** above, and the forbidden gap \(E_g\) between.

| Solid | Band picture | Gap |
|---|---|---|
| **Conductor** | Conduction and valence bands **overlap**, or the valence band is only partly filled — there is no forbidden region between them | \(E_g \approx 0\) |
| **Semiconductor** | A small gap; the conduction band is empty at \(0\) K and the valence band full | \(E_g < 3\) eV (Si \(1{\cdot}1\) eV, Ge \(0{\cdot}7\) eV) |
| **Insulator** | A wide gap; conduction band empty, valence band full | \(E_g > 3\) eV (diamond \(\approx 6\) eV) |

**Which band determines conductivity.**

The **conduction band** — more exactly, how many electrons are in it and how easily they can be put there, which is decided by the width of the gap below it.

An electron in a completely full band cannot conduct, whatever field is applied: there is no unoccupied state of slightly higher energy for it to move into. Only a **partly filled** band carries current. A conductor's conduction band is partly occupied already, so it conducts at any temperature; an insulator's is empty and its gap is far too wide for thermal energy to bridge, so it does not.

The scale of the comparison is what decides everything: thermal energy at room temperature is \(kT \approx 0{\cdot}026\) eV. That is negligible against an insulator's \(6\) eV but not against a semiconductor's \(1\) eV, because the occupancy depends on \(E_g\) **exponentially**, not linearly.

**Effect of rising temperature on a semiconductor.**

The conductivity **increases**, and sharply.

\(\sigma = e(n_e\mu_e + n_h\mu_h)\)

Heating supplies energy that breaks covalent bonds. Each broken bond sends an electron up into the conduction band and leaves a hole behind in the valence band, so \(n_e\) and \(n_h\) both rise — roughly as

\(n_i \propto e^{-E_g/2kT}\)

The mobilities \(\mu_e\) and \(\mu_h\) actually *fall* with temperature, because the hotter lattice scatters carriers more. But that decrease is a weak power law and the rise in carrier number is exponential, so the carrier term wins comfortably and \(\sigma\) rises.

**This is the reverse of a metal**, and the contrast is the point of the question. A metal already has all the carriers it will ever have; heating only increases lattice scattering, so its resistance **rises**. A semiconductor gains carriers faster than it loses mobility, so its resistance **falls**. That is why a semiconductor is said to have a *negative* temperature coefficient of resistance, and why a thermistor makes a sensitive thermometer.

rows.stem:
How is the spacing between fringes in a double slit experiment affected if :
(i) the slits separation is increased,
(ii) the colour of light used is changed from red to blue,
(iii) the whole apparatus is submerged in a oil of refractive index 1.2 ?
Justify your anwer in each case.
rows.solution:
The fringe spacing in Young's double-slit experiment is

\(\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}\)

so every part of this question is read off one formula — provided the right \(\lambda\) is used in part (iii).

**(i) The slit separation is increased.**

\(\beta \propto \dfrac{1}{d}\), so the spacing **decreases**; doubling \(d\) halves \(\beta\).

*Why.* The path difference between the two slits at a given angle is \(d\sin\theta\). Widening \(d\) makes that difference reach \(\lambda\) at a smaller angle, so successive maxima are crowded closer together on the screen. This is also the practical reason the two slits must be close: separate them too far and the fringes become too fine to resolve.

**(ii) The colour changes from red to blue.**

\(\beta \propto \lambda\), and \(\lambda_{\text{blue}} < \lambda_{\text{red}}\) — roughly \(450\) nm against \(650\) nm — so the spacing **decreases**, by a factor of about \(1{\cdot}4\).

*Why.* Constructive interference needs a path difference of a whole wavelength; a shorter wavelength meets that condition at a smaller angle, so the pattern shrinks towards the centre.

**(iii) The whole apparatus is submerged in oil of refractive index \(1{\cdot}2\).**

The spacing **decreases**, to \(\beta' = \dfrac{\beta}{1{\cdot}2} \approx 0{\cdot}83\beta\).

*Why.* Moving the apparatus into the oil does not change \(D\) or \(d\), and the **frequency** of the light is unchanged. What changes is the wavelength *inside the medium*:

\(\lambda' = \dfrac{\lambda}{\mu}\)

so

\(\beta' = \dfrac{\lambda' D}{d} = \dfrac{\lambda D}{\mu d} = \dfrac{\beta}{\mu}\)

This is the part where a wrong instinct is common. It is tempting to think the colour, and so the wavelength, is a fixed property of the light. It is not — the **frequency** is fixed, and the wavelength contracts by \(\mu\) in the medium. Interference counts wavelengths along the actual path, so it is the local wavelength that governs the pattern.

**All three changes go the same way**, which is the useful summary: the pattern contracts in every case. And in each case the quantity that really matters is the same one — the angle at which the path difference first reaches one local wavelength.
